title: Linear & Logistic Regression: Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of linear regression, least squares and gradient descent, logistic regression with the sigmoid, MSE and log loss, and L1/L2 regularization. Ordered from mental model to cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Regression Mental Model
points: Linear regression predicts a number: ŷ = w·x + b, a weighted sum of features plus a bias
Learning means choosing w and b that minimize a loss over the training data
Residual = y − ŷ; the fit line is the one with the smallest total squared residuals
Logistic regression predicts a probability for a class: p = σ(w·x + b), then thresholds it (default 0.5)
Both are linear models: the decision boundary of logistic regression is a straight line (hyperplane) w·x + b = 0

chapters.title: Least Squares and Gradient Descent
points: Least squares minimizes the sum of squared residuals Σ(y − ŷ)²
Normal equation gives the closed-form solution: w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy
Normal equation costs about O(n·d²+d³) and fails when XᵀX is singular (collinear features); use it for small d
Gradient descent update: w ← w − α·∂L/∂w, repeated until the loss stops falling
Learning rate α: too large diverges, too small crawls; always scale features (standardize) so descent converges fast
Batch uses all rows per step, SGD uses one, mini-batch uses a small chunk (the default in practice)

chapters.title: Sigmoid and Logistic Regression
points: Sigmoid σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^−z) squashes any real z into (0, 1); σ(0) = 0.5
Logit (log-odds) = ln(p / (1 − p)) = w·x + b: the model is linear in log-odds
Each weight is a log-odds change: e^w is the odds ratio for a one-unit increase in that feature
Gradient of log loss w.r.t. w is Xᵀ(p − y)/n, the same form as linear regression's gradient
The threshold 0.5 is a choice: lower it to favor recall, raise it to favor precision
Perfectly separable data makes the weights grow without bound unless regularized

chapters.title: Loss Functions: MSE and Log Loss
points: MSE = (1/n)·Σ(y − ŷ)²: convex for linear regression, penalizes large errors quadratically, sensitive to outliers
MAE and Huber are the outlier-robust alternatives to MSE
Log loss (binary cross-entropy) = −(1/n)·Σ[y·ln p + (1−y)·ln(1−p)]
Log loss punishes confident wrong predictions very heavily: p = 0.01 when y = 1 costs −ln 0.01 ≈ 4.6
Never use MSE for logistic regression: with the sigmoid it is non-convex and gives weak gradients; log loss is convex
Clip probabilities to [ε, 1−ε] to avoid ln 0 = −∞

chapters.title: Regularization: L1 and L2
points: Regularization adds a penalty on weights to the loss to fight overfitting: L = loss + λ·penalty
L2 (Ridge) penalty is λ·Σw²: shrinks weights smoothly toward zero but rarely makes them exactly zero
L1 (Lasso) penalty is λ·Σ|w|: drives some weights exactly to zero, giving built-in feature selection
L1's diamond-shaped constraint hits the axes (sparse); L2's circular one does not
Larger λ means more bias and less variance; choose λ by cross-validation (scikit-learn LogisticRegression uses C = 1/λ)
Standardize features before regularizing, and never penalize the bias term
Elastic Net mixes L1 and L2 and handles correlated features better than L1 alone

chapters.title: Regression Cheat Sheet
points: Linear: ŷ = Xw + b; logistic: p = σ(Xw + b); loss MSE vs log loss
Gradient descent: w ← w − α·Xᵀ(ŷ − y)/n for both models (with ŷ = p for logistic)
Normal equation w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy for small d; gradient descent for large d or logistic
MSE for regression, log loss for classification; MAE or Huber when outliers dominate
L2 shrinks, L1 selects, Elastic Net does both; tune λ by cross-validation
Pre-flight checklist: standardize features, check the learning-rate curve, hold out a validation set, pick the threshold from precision vs recall
